note: Locked demo cases, one per advertised one-pager bullet plus the executive framing. Phrased the way a Chief Compliance Officer or Trading Desk Supervisor actually talks - nobody types an operation name.

cases.onepager_bullet: pain: manual review created delays and increased audit risk
cases.prompt: Are we going to fail our next MiFID audit? What's actually broken on the desk right now?
cases.assertion_note: Assert ONLY on identifiers the agent computed (trader ids). The LLM's prose varies run to run, so thematic words like 'reporting' or regime names like 'RTS 22' make a good answer flake red. Entities are stable because they come from the agent, not the model.

cases.onepager_bullet: Identify upcoming certification expirations and enroll traders
cases.prompt: Which of my traders can't legally trade today, and who do I have to call?

cases.onepager_bullet: Scan all executed trades for reporting accuracy, required fields, and best-execution performance
cases.prompt: We executed a few hundred trades this week. Which ones will the regulator reject, and why exactly?
Is anything about to go live that shouldn't?

cases.onepager_bullet: Automate corrections and submissions to the regulatory portal
cases.prompt: My head of trading says the reporting is fine. Prove him wrong with specifics I can take to the board.

assertion_principle: The tool description and parameters are the ONLY context the Brainstem has about this agent. So: expects_agent proves the description was sufficient to route; must_include is asserted against the agent's own output (deterministic, never the model's prose); must_not_include catches stalls that prove the agent was never called. A routing failure is a defect in the description, not flakiness.
